source.title_on_document: The Creative Link Between Words and Ideas is Weakening in the AI Era

paper_design_summary: Four preregistered natural experiments compare personal-statement admissions essays submitted to four U.S. universities before (2018-2022 cycles) and after (2024-2025 cycles) the release of ChatGPT, scoring each essay on word-level diversity (DSI), within-essay sentence-level diversity, document-level distinctness from the nearest other essay in the cohort, and a creativity rating from a GPT-4.1-mini model fine-tuned on expert ratings. Supporting analyses compare 1,500 human essays with 1,500 GPT-5-mini essays, relate 22 experts' creativity ratings of 370 human essays to the three metrics, and test LLM raters with 0 to 128 reference essays. In a within-subjects study, 203 students at one university uploaded their original admissions essay and wrote two prompts; the researchers ran the prompts through GPT-4.1 to produce an AI-revised and an AI-generated essay, and the three essays per student were compared on the same three metrics. No one was randomly assigned to AI.

outcomes.name: Word-level diversity (Divergent Semantic Integration, DSI)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean semantic distance between all word pairs within one essay, using bert-large-uncased layers 6-7 embeddings; standardized within institution using pooled data across cycles excluding 2023. A within-essay lexical diversity measure, not a comparison across people. Robustness: full unbalanced sample (Table S6), event-time models (Table S10a), COVID-period models (Table S11a), models with controls (Table S12a).

contrasts.reported: Post 0.16 (0.98) vs pre -0.08 (1.00), standardized z (SD); n = 23,760 post, 47,520 pre essays; Welch t = 30.43, df = 48291.34; Cohen's d = 0.24 [0.23, 0.26]; p < .001. Full sample (Table S6): d = 0.20 [0.18, 0.21].
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 52 (supp. p. 26), Table S9; PDF p. 8, Fig. 1; PDF p. 46 (supp. p. 20), Table S6

outcomes.name: Sentence-level diversity (mean pairwise distance between sentence embeddings within an essay)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean pairwise cosine distance between sentence embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) within one essay; standardized as for O1. Measures variation of ideas within a single essay, not across people. Robustness variants as for O1.

contrasts.locator: PDF p. 52 (supp. p. 26), Table S9; PDF p. 8, Fig. 1

outcomes.name: Document-level distinctness (minimum pairwise distance to the nearest other essay in the cohort)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: For each essay, the smallest cosine distance between its document embedding (OpenAI text-embedding-3-large) and those of all other essays in the same admissions cycle; standardized as for O1. Higher = more distinct from other applicants' essays. Robustness variants as for O1.

contrasts.locator: PDF p. 52 (supp. p. 26), Table S9; PDF p. 8, Fig. 1

diversity_detail.metric: Minimum pairwise cosine distance (document-level distinctness); higher = more diverse, so no sign reversal
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each essay against all other essays in the same admissions cycle at the same university (nearest neighbor); cycles balanced to 11,880 essays each by random sampling
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Welch's t-test on essay-level standardized scores (essays treated as independent)
diversity_detail.notes: Defined in Table S1 (PDF p. 31, supp. p. 5) and PDF pp. 29-30 (supp. pp. 3-4).

outcomes.name: Creativity rating by expert-tuned GPT-4.1-mini (total effect of post-ChatGPT period)

outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-4.1-mini fine-tuned on 22 experts' percentile creativity ratings of 370 pre-ChatGPT essays (r = .82 with expert ratings on 111 held-out essays). studies.label: Controlled Experiment 3: within-subjects comparison of each student's original essay, AI-revised essay, and AI-generated essay

assignment.what_was_assigned: Not randomized. Every participant contributes three essays: the original admissions essay they had submitted (human-written), an essay GPT-4.1 produced from the participant's revision prompt plus original essay, and an essay GPT-4.1 produced from the participant's generation prompt. Participants wrote the generation prompt and then the revision prompt; researchers ran the prompts after data collection, so participants never saw or edited AI output.

eligibility.reason: No study randomly assigns people to AI. The four natural experiments and the pilot compare essays before and after ChatGPT's release (observational; AI use unobserved). Controlled Experiment 3 has 203 people but no randomization: each student's original essay is compared with GPT-4.1 essays that the researchers produced from the student's prompts, and no participant used or saw AI output (coded ai_vs_human). Controlled Experiment 1 compares human and GPT-5-mini essays; Controlled Experiment 2 is model-only. Outcomes are computed on the essays (embedding metrics, fine-tuned LLM creativity score).

one_line_finding: Across four universities, post-ChatGPT admissions essays showed higher word-level diversity (Cohen's d 0.15 to 0.39) but lower within-essay sentence-level diversity (d -0.18 to -0.06) and lower document-level distinctness from other essays (d -0.15 to -0.07) (PDF p. 52, Table S9), and GPT-4.1 essays built from 203 students' prompts were less distinct than their originals (AI-generated -1.52 SD, AI-revised -0.98 SD; PDF p. 89, Table S16).
open_questions: Design class of Controlled Experiment 3: coded ai_vs_human because researchers ran participants' prompts through GPT-4.1 and no participant saw or edited AI output; it could be argued as quasi_people (non-random within-person comparison of a person's own essay with AI versions directed by that person's prompts), in which case the word and sentence outcomes would be with_ai and the document outcome across_people.
Natural experiments count essays (applications), not people; each essay presumably comes from one applicant, but the paper does not report a count of people, so people counts are left null.
Whether the post-ChatGPT period counts as 'AI available' for coding ai_available_when_produced: AI was available but use is unobserved and prohibited by application platforms; coded 'mixed'.
notes: Page map: PDF pp. 1-26 are the main text (printed pages 1-26); PDF pp. 27-89 are the supplement (printed supp. pages 1-63; PDF page = supp. page + 26). Inconsistencies noticed: (1) main text says CE3 participants' original essays were submitted 'all prior to 2022' (PDF p. 16), but the supplement says 72 sophomores applied during the transitional period and 31 freshmen applied after ChatGPT (PDF p. 86); (2) ChatGPT release given as November 30, 2022 (PDF p. 32) and November 22, 2022 in footnote 1 (PDF p. 32); (3) Table S6 caption says all Welch tests p < .001, but the selective liberal-arts sentence-level full-sample row shows t = -1.67, d = -0.02 [-0.04, 0.00] (PDF p. 46). The abstract's 372,793 essays equals the four balanced analytic samples (313,388) plus the three excluded 2023 cycles (59,405). Further robustness outputs not listed as separate outcomes: event-time models (Tables S10a-c), COVID-period models (S11a-d), models with controls (S12a-d), subgroup interactions (S13a-e, Fig. 2), word-to-document association changes (S14b-c). Controlled Experiment 1 reports only correlations among the metrics within human (n = 1,500) and GPT (n = 1,500) essays (e.g., word-document r = .117 human vs -.283 GPT; PDF p. 77, Table S14a), not differences in levels, so no outcome is listed.
